This is our last craft fair of the 2022 season and we're excited to share the bounty of our final harvest with you. Winter is coming, and this may be one of the last truly beautiful weekends to enjoy outdoors. We know it's not even Halloween yet, but our fair is just 70 days before Christmas and it really is incredible how quickly those days pass with so many holidays to celebrate and decorate. If you're looking for decor, self-pampering items, and beautiful handmade gifts from home-based artisans, our craft fair vendors will have you covered at our last craft fair of the season.

Happy anniversary to us! We've come so far in just one year and this event will be a celebration of the resilience of this community.

After surviving the Porter County Master Gardener's Garden Walk in June last year, we decided to start a monthly event, inviting crafters to set up tents along side our farm stand, giving walking tours of our property and gardens, and trying to bring that festival feeling into our community. Just another one of those crazy ideas from the folks at BCF.

And it sure has been a crazy ride. Only four vendors and a few dozen customers decided to take a chance on us at that first event. We got frustrated and discouraged but we kept pushing through with the support of a wonderful community of people who believed in us. We've been growing and improving every month ever since. We've tripled our parking lot space, expanded to a little over two miles of beautiful walking trails, and more than quadrupled the number of vendors who want to be part of this experience. All we need to keep growing is for you to be part of this - tell your friends and family!

This is our third Craft Fair for the 2022 season, and I can tell already that it's going to be even better than the last one. This is a great opportunity to support your entrepreneurial neighbors and invest in our community. Tell your friends to meet you here. item.title: Edge of Liberty Craft Fair - June 19, 2022 - Father's Day
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
James and I were reminiscing the other day about our dads, and realized that much of who we are and what we believe came from the example of these similar but dramatically different guys. One immigrant, one descended from early settlers - both hard-working men who loved their wives, loved people in their community, and did their best to love their children (and we both admit that neither of us made that easy on them). They were both gardeners - one a double digger and one that was practically attached to his tiller - but both so very proud of their tomatoes and grapes. They both loved the outdoors - one poking a fire at a camp site, the other dropping a fishing line into a lake. Neither one of us could ever figure out what to give them for Father's Day while they were alive, but we now both realize that the present they wanted most of all, any day of the year, was presence. Walking together on a hiking trail, scavenging finds at a flea market, checking out booths at a festival, eating together - barely talking but occasionally sharing wonder at simple things like a frog jumping in a pond, discovering deer tracks, or watching a tomato grow.

Give your dad a present he will truly cherish - give him presence and bring him to The Edge of Liberty Craft Fair!

This is our second Craft Fair for the 2022 season - and if you enjoyed the one in May, you're going to love this one. We've doubled the number of vendors and added a food truck with plenty of places to sit and enjoy lunch.

This is a great opportunity to support your entrepreneurial neighbors and invest in our community. Tell your friends to meet you here. Enjoy lunch at our picnic tables near the pond where ducks, geese, sandhill cranes, and eagles have been lunching all spring. Tour our perennial pollinator garden, our market garden, and see what your neighbors have done with their plots so far in our community garden.

Since the Porter County Master Gardener's Garden Walk last year (tickets for this year's walk click here), over a thousand people have walked through our gardens and shopped local with our home-based art and craft vendors and at our farm stand. item.title: Time of Transition
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
As gardeners turned farmers, the ancient celebrations that are part of the Wheel of the Year have an important role in our lives and our planning. While it's not religious for us, the celebrations nearly always have meaning to anyone who cares for the land. Samhain, which has evolved into Halloween and All Souls Day, is the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter. It's a celebration of all of the life and the bounty that the prior season has brought, and a time to reflect on life that has ended wi.

It's easy to see, as you watch your plants turn to dust, how this harvest period became a time to remember the people we love who have passed on and to celebrate the lives they lived. It's a doorway from one cycle of life to another. A time of transition.

For us this year, it's about remembering all we've achieved at Batshit Crazy Farms as we host our very last Market Day ever and to turn our thoughts to renewing our commitment to the ever expanding Edge of Liberty community.

We haven't even finished putting all of our planting areas to bed for the season, and we're already filling our shopping cart at Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds for next year while planning how we're going to plant out our market gardens using the GrowVeg garden planner. Granted, it's been raining all week so sitting at a computer and planning is about all we can do, even though we did take some time out to dig the last of the sweet potatoes out of some very heavy mud before the frost took them. We've also been pureeing and dehydrating hot peppers all week for a special Christmas edition of our famous hot pepper blend.

Thinking ahead to next year...would love to hear our community's feedback on produce you'd like to see us have available that you've not seen at our farm stands before...and certainly some feedback on things you absolutely loved and don't want us to ever stop growing.

Join the conversation in our Facebook group.

And don't forget to come see us one last time at Batshit Crazy Farms Market Day - The Series Finale - today from 9 to 5.

item.title: Reflections of the Season
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
The fall garden has always been a strange place for me. The mix of feelings that wash over me as I take daily walks at the Edge of Liberty to destress after my morning work meetings is sometimes overwhelming.

I am in awe of nature and how it has reacted to the things we do here. A pair of sandhill cranes have claimed the newly dug garlic field - in love with the wheat grass we over-seeded there as a cover crop - and have claimed the pond as their very own. The baby tadpoles that made the pond bubble all spring have grown into full-sized frogs and are quite vocal about their displeasure at being disturbed from their naps in the tall grass. A fox has claimed the bonfire circle as her own having found a lovely overwintering spot among the piles of brush. Butterflies are doing their best at extracting the last bits of nectar from the fennel flowers before they go to seed after having emerged from the milk thistle nearby. The killdeer are back and making noise, scoping out which part of our property they will use as a nesting ground again next spring. Hawks are circling overhead keeping watch over the community garden keeping it clear of bunnies who desperately want the fall crops planted there.

I am grateful for the people who have helped change this abandoned farm into a beautiful place to gather and reflect. I see their hands and hearts and hear their words everywhere. The bright yellow flowers on our sunchokes that came from the people at NWI Permaculture brighten our market garden as the squash plants nearby die back to expose their orange and green fruits. The cool season crop seeds donated to our community gardeners from the Porter County Master Gardeners are still flourishing in the plots that have not yet been cleared and are bright patches of life in the garden. I think of all the new friends we've made amongst our gardeners, and wonder at their journey from novice to seasoned veteran through this challenging season that's drawing to a close. I think of all the people who've come through here for our events this past year, and hope they come back to see the beauty of the fall colors and partake of our surprisingly bountiful harvest at our last Open Farm event of the year.

As I walk, I see so much work yet to be done harvesting and putting our gardens to bed for the winter and I feel both overwhelming despair at ever getting it all done before the snows and energized joy at knowing that my husband and I share such passion for improving the soil and feeding our community that we will prevail together.

As I'm writing these thoughts and reflections of this season that's coming to a close, I'm reminded that less than a year ago I wrote a similar post that contained my dreams for the future of the Edge of Liberty. I just stopped to re-read it, and I'm incredulous that we've come this far so fast. At first I thought, I have no idea how we did it, but that thought was fleeting as it's pretty clear. While I'm the dreamer, schemer, planner, and planter, it was the daily hard work and commitment of the man I took a chance on meeting for a drink fifteen years ago today that made it happen. It is his vision that has shaped the landscape and his hands that forged the paths through it and his strength that protected it from wildlife and kept it watered through the drought.

That guy I met 15 years ago and that place we walked through together five years ago - wild, untamed beauty that few could see - I loved them both at first sight - and love them more every day. I hope to love them and watch them grow together for many more seasons.

When you visit at this year's garden walk, in addition to labelling a lot of the interesting plants, throughout the property we've posted mini stories for you to read and learn. We're posting all the stories here as a blog post so you can read them on your phone. They are in order as you would see them if you walked counter-clockwise around the property from the parking lot.

The Sign

We don’t know who painted this sign or when it was erected, but it’s long enough ago that the metal framing is rusted through in multiple spots and the lettering is fading on the south side. We spent Easter morning 2020 repainting the black letters. A wind storm earlier this year required the addition of zip ties to hold it together.

When we first purchased this property in 2016, it was so overgrown that you couldn’t even see either side of this sign anymore. We didn’t even know it had anything on the north side until we cleared the area.

If anyone has any details about the history of this sign, or knows someone who can lovingly restore it, please talk to us.

What we know so far:

From a verbal conversation with Leroy, a 94 year old World War II veteran who lives nearby:

It’s always been here my whole life. (May 22, 2021)

From a conversation with the Porter County, Indiana - Genealogy and History Facebook page:

I've seen that sign many, many times. Unfortunately, I don't have any specific information concerning its history or the landowner that may have erected the sign. I would love to know its history, however. If you ever remove the sign, then please consider donating it to the Porter County Museum.

Also, where you live was commonly referred to as Gospel Corners prior to 1900. The name derived from the Gospel Corners Methodist Episcopal Church (sometimes called the Flint Lake Methodist Church) that was across 49 from your property. After 1900, it was more commonly referred to as Kinne's Corners. The Gospel Corner's church disbanded after 1867 and the church was razed before 1910.

(July 14, 2020)

So our best guess is that it’s well over 100 years old and was erected by members of the Gospel Corners church.

The Edge of Liberty Story

In 2016, we were asked to sign a petition to try to stop the rezoning of this property from rural residential to office park; hundreds of petition signers didn’t want to lose the rural feeling of Liberty Township. Along with dozens of our neighbors, we attended zoning meetings. But, while they seemed to commiserate with our concerns, no one on the zoning board could find a legal reason to deny the rezoning request. Since the property sale was contingent on the rezoning going through, we “fought city hall” by making an offer with no contingency, and the seller was all too happy to take our offer. He didn’t want to see it developed either. So, with a small real estate investment, we “saved the day” for our community (and our own property values).

But then we were faced with what to do with a four acre abandoned farm that was barely walkable and completely unusable. For the first year, it was just our own private ATV track and a place to walk our dogs. We invested in a brush mower to make walking trails and started discovering the potential of the property, but it was a losing battle. As soon as we cleared an area, it was quickly overrun with new growth.

This is when we started our journey in biomimicry and regenerative agriculture. The complex science of sheet composting with artistically spread layers of wood chips and hours of hard labor, along with the contribution of well over a thousand truck loads from nearly every tree service in the area, have transformed this property from eyesore to destination. Where once there had been invasive scrub brush growing in nutritionally depleted hardpan clay soil, there are now viable gardens growing in enriched soil with their own thriving ecosystems.

Our long term goal is to “retire” as professional farmers and we’ve been pursuing education from Purdue University to learn what we need to know to transition from gardener to farmer.

About Us

James & Nancy live in a home in an adjacent subdivision. There they have a tenth acre vegetable garden that was part of the 2019 Garden Walk. For a number of years, they have been selling produce from their home at a weekly farm stand with a “pay what you can, when you can” pricing model to help out their neighbors in need, while making sure that the excess from the garden they built to feed and educate their now adult sons doesn’t go to waste.

They moved to this area from Elkhart and Chicago respectively 25 years ago, and have fully embraced Liberty Township and its rural nature as their home. They want to see The Edge of Liberty grow as a destination enthusiastically supported by and in support of the community, loved by locals, and visited by tourists to celebrate life and create happiness.

You can learn more at our website https://edge-of-liberty.com or follow us on Facebook at https://fb.me/TheEdgeOfLibertyIN

Community Garden

Since we purchased this property to preserve our rural community, it’s only right that we share some of it with the community.

This is our first season with a Community Garden at The Edge of Liberty. From our blog November 25, 2020:

While taking our daily walk around the property last week, I "convinced" my husband that a community garden in the middle of the turnaround hoop was the best use of the plot he's been amending with neighborhood leaf collection this fall. I put "convinced" in air quotes because he still has his doubts that it would be a successful endeavor, and is probably a little sad that it means 625 fewer delicata squash plants growing next season. I wasn't sure it would be successful either, but with one post on Nextdoor.com, within two days I had nearly all of the 16 plots claimed.

We subsequently decided to expand another 25 feet to the east to make 24 plots because online interest had been so encouraging.

The area was amended with leaves collected from a nearby neighborhood in the fall, and an additional 1200 cubic feet of compost in the early spring, before dividing up into 10x10 plots.

It’s especially challenging to manage a plot at this garden since we have no running water. Stewards must keep an eye on the weather and water by hand regularly. This past month has been tough on all of our gardens and our gardeners.

There is no charge for plots and the rules are simple - no chemicals, no perennials, no permanent structures, and no visitors except during Open Farm events. Stewards can keep what they grow, and are just asked to clear out by the end of October so we can amend the soil with leaf collection for next season.

Next: Exit at the gate and proceed to the Market Garden gate directly across the “street”

Market Garden

This fenced area has 22 forty-foot long rows planted with a variety of vegetables including asparagus, strawberries, four kinds of winter squash, sweet peppers, mini melons, zucchini/summer squash, five different chilies, slicing and cherry tomatoes, watermelons, kale, sunchokes, potatoes, garlic, rhubarb, cucumbers, ground cherries, and sweet potatoes.

This is our fourth year planting in this area, and each year has been an opportunity to learn from failure. Initially this area was overrun with grapevines, blackberries, russian olive, and sumac miraculously growing in lifeless soil as hard as a brick. After a year of clearing and adding wood chips to suppress weed growth, we tried our hand at growing a pumpkin patch. We planted too late in the season. The following year, we planted earlier and added a larger variety of squash, melons, watermelons, beans, and tomatoes...and fed the deer. Last year we invested in fencing to keep out the critters and were rewarded with drought. This year we invested in an irrigation pond to collect rain water and gravity fed drip irrigation. The lack of rain this year has been beyond frustrating as there’s been barely enough to keep the ecosystem in the pond thriving, so we’ve had to bring water from home nearly daily to replenish the barrels.

All the while, we continuously replenish the wood chips in the walking paths and their decomposition over the last five years has brought life back to the soil and helps with moisture retention.

Our long-term goal with this property is to make it a real, thriving business that we can manage after “retiring,” and at the center of it is this market garden. Short term, we’ll be selling produce from a farm stand here during Open Farm events the rest of the season.

Next: Exit on the west end near the strawberries to visit the Pollinator Garden

Pollinator Garden

2020 was a weird year, and everyone did crazy things to cope. Our pandemic project was this garden. The design is a 50x50 plot with two concentric hexagonal paths and four intersecting radial paths to create eight triangular raised beds and eight trapezoids that we could fill with flowering herbs and perennials that pollinators love.

As with the market garden, it was overgrown with invasives and the soil was hardpan clay. Early in the season we got a lot of rain and the paths we were digging held so much water that we nicknamed the area Atlantis. When it dried out enough to proceed, the soil was too hard to work.

We had to take shortcuts to finish the project and are paying for incomplete weed removal this year. In some cases, we’re embracing the weeds and taming patches of wild blackberries along the outer perimeter, and encouraging creeping charlie, monarda, goldenrod, and milk thistle on the west end. We also battle weeds of our own making, constantly rehoming volunteer sunflowers, chamomile, primrose, and last year’s hollyhocks.

All of the plantings are clearly labeled and can be viewed from the center of the garden. At the ends of paths not hosting a gate or a beehive are fruit trees (paw paw, Asian pear) grown from seed.

As for the bees, all of the hives here are currently empty. Keeping bees at our home was no longer viable with residential mosquito spraying services employed by a number of our neighbors, so we moved them here. Our colonies did not overwinter and we have not seen a single wild honey bee this season, even though this garden is teeming with other pollinators on a regular basis.

Next: Exit by the “back door” on the south end near the perennial onions and cilantro.

Compost

We’ve built a compost bin for use by our community gardeners as an easy place for them to dispose of weeds, plant refuse, and thinnings, and as a storage location for finished compost that they can use to amend their plots. The bin was built in early spring out of free pallets and reclaimed lumber all sourced on social media.

Since the bin is new this year, the finished compost provided was hauled in from the Valparaiso compost site managed by Porter County Recycling and Waste Reduction.

The majority of composting we have done on this property is sheet composting. We try to never leave any soil bare and use thick layers of wood chips to prepare areas for future garden plots. We try to plan three years in advance as it takes at least that long for wood chips to break down into gorgeous black gold soil.

The area just south of the pollinator garden is currently being prepared for an expanded orchard which will not be purchased and planted until after cicada Brood XIII in 2024. Currently our fruit production efforts have been limited to what we’ve planted in the outer perimeter of the pollinator garden, and attempts to prune back to health the established apple and pear trees on the property so that we can use them for root stock in future grafting projects.

Next: This is the last of the formal gardens on this property, but you’re encouraged to wander and explore the other three acres to see random plantings and native discoveries if you’re up for a long walk.

Take a ← left to return to your vehicle, a right → to continue the tour through shaded areas of reclaimed fruit trees, saved natives and marginally controlled invasives, or straight ahead to see the corn field and pond. Stay on the wood chip paths or mown areas to avoid poison ivy.

Fruit Trees & Vines

Our long term goal is to have a relatively healthy orchard on this property. Over the course of the last few years we have discovered - and saved from invasive vines - a number of crabapple and pear trees that we hope to be able to use as a base for that plan. This is the first year that we’ve seen heavy fruiting on any of them since they had spent years blocked from cross-pollinating each other.

As we’re clearing out the overgrowth on the property, and returning trees to health, we always give priority to anything that flowers and can help the pollinators flourish.

We have had some success starting Asian pears from seed, and one of our community gardeners has supplied us with fig and paw paw saplings that he was able to propagate.

Additionally this property is blessed with healthy Allegheny blackberries, some of them heavily fruiting on second-year wood since they’re in an area not recently cleared. Unfortunately, the property is also cursed with wild grape vines intent on killing trees and making nearly inedible grapes.

We attempted to self-teach grafting on some of the smaller crabapple trees with cuttings from our home, but all of our grafts failed. Likely we didn’t store our cuttings properly between collection and attachment, or we did not seal the grafts completely. Heavy winds in the early spring dislodged many of them. All of the scions dried out and died before they could connect.

We also hope to learn about air-layering to propagate some of the peach trees at our home before they reach the end of their twelve year life span. Air layering is a method of propagating new trees and shrubs from stems still attached to the parent plant. The stem is wrapped with damp moss to encourage roots to form.

Native and Invasive

We’re always discovering new plants that grow here naturally and we do our best to give them space to flourish, even plants people normally consider weeds.

Some things we originally considered beautiful (autumn olive/Russian olive) we’ve since learned are invasives, while others that we had considered nuisances to be eradicated (goldenrod, blackberries) are native to the area.

Our top goal since acquiring this property has been eradicating the vines that are killing the trees. Whenever we find a tree worth saving, we clear the area immediately around it and then pile it high with wood chips. When we’re certain that the undergrowth is dead, we can pull the chips away from the tree to give it room to breathe. If you look up into the canopy of many of our healthiest trees, you can see the remnants of the vines that tried to kill them.

Our tree saving efforts prioritized evergreens first, followed by flowering trees for the pollinators, and then the black walnuts which are the largest shade trees on the property.

Whenever we intentionally bring in a non-native species (daylilies, hibiscus, iris), we do our best to control its spread with clear borders and seed pod control. There are a number of non-natives that were brought here by prior landowners that have since gone feral that we keep under control but don’t try to eradicate, like garlic and flowering alliums.

We still have a lot of work ahead of us to get the invasives under control and to save the native plants. We also still have a lot of learning to do to understand which is which and how to achieve our personal goals while still keeping in tune with nature.

Three sisters

The three sisters is an ancient method of companion planting used by Native Americans throughout North America in multiple variations.

“Sister Beans” deposit nitrogen from the air into the soil, in a form that the plants can use. The beans will use the corn as support, so we needed to wait to plant it until the corn is about knee high. Because of our recent lack of rain, this was a very long wait.

“Sister Corn” provides support for bean vines to climb upon, and is a heavy nitrogen feeder. Planted alone as a monocrop, it rapidly depletes the soil of water and nutrients and needs its sisters to thrive.

“Sister Squash” shades the ground with its large leaves to provide a good growing environment for all the sisters. Raccoons and other animals find the texture of their foliage to be uncomfortable and avoid the area.

We set aside one plot in the community garden to plant the three sisters in the traditional mounding method with all three plants very close together as an experiment to see if it’s significantly different to the row method we employed here.

Here we’ve planted bantam corn, romano beans, and acorn squash. In early May we planted the corn in rows in a freshly tilled field. In late May we seeded the squash as a perimeter around the field. Once the corn was knee high, we seeded beans in alternate rows to feed the growing corn.

Because this garden is unfenced, it’s quite likely it will become deer food, but if it keeps their interest away from the fenced gardens it’s done its job.

You Can’t Save Them All

This tree, like many others we’ve cut down on this property, was killed by invasive vines. No matter how pretty a vine looks climbing up a tree, cut it at its roots as soon as you can.

When vines get big and spread, they suffocate the tree. Their leaves block air and light from the bark, and the vine's roots compete with the tree for nutrients in the soil below it. The vines have hairs that clasp onto and attach themselves to the bark, which puts more stress on the tree.

Pond

The property slopes to the southwest and all of our runoff was regularly flooding our neighbors yards and overflowing the retaining ponds in the Wild Rose subdivision. The graveyard just beyond our southwest corner was frequently under water.

Last August we had a rain catchment dug out with the south and west edges bermed to stop the flow of water that was making us bad neighbors.

Since the soil on this property is practically pure clay, it didn’t need to be lined to quickly evolve into a pond with its own ecosystem.

While it started out being little more than a large mud puddle used by birds to bathe and the occasional deer watering hole, it’s now home to a painted turtle (Nessie), three mallards (Fillmore, Mallory, and Maleficent), and about a million tadpoles. If it looks like the pond water is boiling, that’s just the baby frogs letting out air or water striders about to become lunch for the turtle.

Earlier this year, we planted irises, daylilies, and hibiscus just beyond the ridges and expect to have a gorgeous display of color next season. We also seeded the southern downslope with buckwheat to encourage deer browse over there rather than in our gardens.

We seeded the entire area with white clover for erosion control to keep the runoff from muddying the water. We regularly “treat” the water with bales of hay to modify the pH of the water to allow the suspended clay to settle out of it.

We believe Nessie and Mallory have laid eggs nearby, so please be careful and watch where you walk. The tadpoles are rapidly turning into tiny little frogs so try not to step on them.

Bee Swarm Traps

Throughout the property you will see mauve colored boxes hanging from trees. These are baited with pheromone in an attempt to capture a feral swarm of honey bees. Captured local swarms have a better chance of survival in our winter weather than purchased packages, which usually come in from California or Georgia where they are used heavily in pollination services. Purchased bees are not adapted to our climate and are usually riddled with disease due to the poor management practices of commercial beekeepers and covered with pesticides and herbicides from the farming practices of their clients. Our success rate in prior years of capturing feral swarms has been quite good, but often we capture them too late in the year to get a young queen. The colonies that we’ve hived die out gradually as the old queen stops laying mid winter and does not maintain a large enough population to keep them all warm through to spring. We don’t consider ourselves beekeepers but pollinator allies and do whatever we can to encourage native pollinators to help our vegetables grow.

Rolling in Clover

In front of you is a gorgeous green lawn where less than a year ago was a bulldozed mass of dirt dug out from the bottom of the pond. A small miracle considering the lack of rain this spring and the fact the soil was 100% heavy clay.

The miracle’s name is white clover. We initially chose to plant it here for the small white flowers to attract pollinators, but as we watched it grow we researched and learned so much about this wonderful plant.

It’s a robust, resilient and competitive legume that builds soil by fixing nitrogen, which in turn feeds the surrounding grass making the lawn even more lush and green. It outcompetes weeds, withstands mowing very well, and holds up to heavy traffic - even deer. As a bonus, when you mulch mow it, the leaves contain so much moisture that it effectively waters the surrounding grass.

White clover has a very thick root system that breaks up and prevents soil compaction, even in our heavy clay. The extensive root system controls erosion and keeps our pond from getting muddier after a rain.

More importantly, it’s incredibly drought-tolerant and requires no additional watering.

Sunflowers

Young sunflowers follow the sun through their travels from east to west, and overnight turn their faces east to wait for the rising sun. It’s a myth that they look at each other on cloudy days (but it does make a lovely meme).

Mature sunflowers stop tracking the sun once their stems firm up and face east all the time. Bees and other beneficial insects love warmth, and blossoms that face east in the morning attract five times more pollinators than those that don’t.

We like that they face east because we’re on the west side of Calumet, and we like to create a little bit of happiness for the commuters who pass us every day.

This massive wall of sunflowers is 250 feet long and is comprised of gray striped mammoth sunflowers that we’ve been saving seeds from for the last 20 years.

Biomimicry

Biomimicry studies nature's models and imitates them or uses them as inspiration for designs or processes with the goal of solving human problems. The problem we had here was lifeless, dry soil and persistent weeds.

We could have just bulldozed everything flat and tilled, but that would be lifeless and boring and do very little for soil health. We chose instead to mimic the conditions of the forest floor, heavily covered in organic material and teeming with life.

What we do here is a little more involved. It’s a little bit science and a little bit art, and with a lot of our own labor and the contributions of many tree services in the area - almost completely free.

You need an artist’s eye. You need to be able to envision what it will look like in the future. As the chips break down into compost, it changes the grade of the land. You have to picture how water flows and direct it to where it’s wanted and away from where it’s not. You’re nature’s interior designer, creating rooms with wood chip borders. You’re a curator framing nature’s art with wood chip frames. You’re a choreographer leading future visitors to all the destinations you created with beautifully curved paths.

As a scientist, you have to know what each load of wood chips you have delivered will do. If you get it in the spring or summer and it’s full of green leaves, it will break down rapidly and generate heat - this is the perfect load for piling on an invasive tree stump or weed patch to “burn” it out. But you have to be careful not to lay it on too thickly so it doesn’t turn to ash. Hardwoods break down more slowly than softwoods, so you have to adjust thickness and uniformity to compensate. Pine will lower soil pH - great for a first application on top of alkaline clay, but not something you want near your established gardens unless you’re growing something acid-loving. Black walnut is poisonous to many plants, but it’s beautiful and long wearing and perfect for paths.

We’re building a whole ecosystem and when applying mulch you have to keep in mind the effects you're going to have on that life-filled soil. It’s more than just dumping wood chips.

Watering Systems

In the market garden we have four water barrels connected in series feeding into a gravity fed drip irrigation system from DripDepot.com. The last barrel has a vermicompost “tea bag” for fertilizing. The community garden uses two barrels and gardeners come regularly to water their plots with a watering can. Eventually these barrels will be filled with rainwater collected in the pond, but as the pond still doesn’t have the depth to support draining, we’ve been bringing in water from our well at home less than a mile away.

item.title: Cooped Up
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
Poor chickens have been cooped up for over a week due to the blizzard and now are venturing out to eat snow because it's easier than trying to get to the water bowl, which is frozen solid anyway.

We don't expect to see temperatures above freezing in the 10 day forecast. Only a few of those days are showing positive double digits.

It's not just the chickens feeling cooped up. It's driving us a little bit crazy too.

All winter long, whenever the weather would allow, we've taking a quick drive up to the farm with our hound dog, Hank, and taken a walk about. Hank is there purely to figure out where the rabbits and moles have been and might still be. It is his personal mission to sniff them out and dig them out of the snow. Sadly, he has yet to figure out that letting out a loud howl when he smells something is a sure fire way to ensure that they won't be there when he gets there to start digging.

We've been playing a bit of a game this winter to see if and when we can walk on the pond. That was some time last week. It will most definitely still be that way with the current temperatures so there's no reason for us to go check on that.

This is our first full winter with a greenhouse, and we were thrilled that with just a little bit of overnight heating, we'd been able to keep many of the cool weather plant starts out there to soak up the sunshine. The daytime temps in the greenhouse have regularly exceeded 80 degrees and on particularly sunny days have gotten into the 100s. But that space heater has really only been able to keep the night time temps 10-15 degrees warmer than the outdoor temps.

Ten degrees was not going to be enough to keep it above freezing the next couple weeks, so we had to move all of our starts back inside the house for the foreseeable future. Our family room has been transformed.

We're trying to find things to occupy our time stuck inside our house for a couple weeks. Today we'll be canning the tomatoes we put in the freezer at the end of the season. Perhaps tomorrow we'll be grinding and bottling the herbs that have been drying in the basement. Maybe we'll even start a carboy of grape wine.

And even though I imagine we'll do better than the chickens in keeping ourselves occupied I can't help but commiserate with them during this unpleasant weather.

I can't wait until we can take Hank back to the farm. Neither can he.

item.title: Beginning Farmer?
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
We're taking a class right now with Purdue University called "Beginning Farmer - How to Plan, Support and Grow your Farm" and we've already seen the benefit that we wanted to get out of it. We needed this to force us to talk about the future and come up with common goals for The Edge of Liberty.

But the thought that goes through my head as we're in break-out discussion groups is - are we really beginners? We've been working on an ever-expanding garden on our residential property for almost twenty-five years. The day we finished expanding it to exactly 4,444 square feet is the day we named it Batshit Crazy Farms.

A tenth of an acre barely qualifies as a farm, but the amount of organic food we were able to produce using raised beds, square foot gardening, succession planting, inter-cropping, and vertical growing methods quickly became over-whelming. It didn't help that our adult sons graduated college and moved out, creating more chicken food than we had chickens to feed.

We tried giving it away and often resorted to a weekly game of ding-dong-ditch leaving vegetables at our neighbors' doorsteps. It wasn't until we set up a weekly farm-stand with an anonymous donation honor box that we felt that our efforts were worth it.

The joy we felt at sharing the fruits of our labors with our neighborhood from our home garden inspired us to start The Edge of Liberty story.

In 2016, we had an opportunity to purchase four acres at the end of our subdivision which was about to be rezoned commercial. We didn't want to lose the rural feeling of our neighborhood by having so much traffic and asphalt where corn fields and goldenrod should be. We didn't have a plan for it other than to just stop the city from progressing northward into our little bit of heaven.

We invested in a brush mower and cleared an area. We spread wood chips to stop the regrowth of the persistent yellow rocket, blackberries, wild rose, and feral grapevines and to try to get some organic material there to break down the rock hard clay soil. The next year we grew pumpkins and melons there but the lack of fencing and the lack of decent soil made it a near-futile effort.

We've never been quitters, so we used the money we made from our farm-stand to invest in fencing and cattle panel trellising and set out to take this little patch of land to the next level. We knew that the pandemic would be the source of food insecurity in our community and we wanted to make sure that we had enough to support our neighbors in need. We concentrated on planting squashes and sweet potatoes to provide the most food value along with things we knew sold well at our farm stand, but by mid summer it became clear that the lack of irrigation was our next hurdle.

We did our best using water we brought from our home and collected from the shed roof from the rare rain showers, but it became clear we needed to do something more. The property was sloped away from the garden, so run off would head to the far corner, flooding our neighbors yards whenever it rained. In September we found a guy with a bulldozer who carved out a beautiful catch basin that has slowly evolved from mud puddle to something that could almost be called a pond. We hope that the thaw and spring rains will bring it all the way to true pond status.

The next challenge is figuring out how to get the thousands of gallons of water we're retaining in that pond to the garden almost five hundred feet away without electricity. We also don't know how to properly distribute it to the planting rows that after three years of sheet composting are no longer made of rock hard clay but have gorgeous black soil. We also don't know how we're going to pay for it all, or how we'll ever make back that investment. We need a better place to store the tractor we purchased than in our garage a mile away. We need a gathering place for the people who will be visiting weekly to work on their plots in our community garden. We need a permanent structure to move our farm stand out of our neighborhood and out to the more accessible location right off the main road. We need a way to extend our season with covered growing spaces beyond what we can achieve in our small greenhouse at our home.

All of these challenges are things that a farmer would know how to overcome. They're complex business challenges that no matter how many years of gardening experience we have, we're ill-equipped to address without education and networking. There is so much we need to learn if we're ever going to be 100% self-employed doing what we love.

So yes, we're beginners at running an agricultural business; and that's the real difference between being a gardener and a farmer.

item.title: Black Friday Bonfire
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
Bonfire event started out a little slow as it was just James and me for the first few hours. We made the most of it, burning through the slightly more dangerous branches that still had leaves attached. It had been wet for a few days prior so we didn't have to chase down all the flying cinders, but we made a game of it anyway.

We polished off a bottle of our 2016 Valkyrie mead, made from honey from a dead out that spring. We were buzzing like bees by the time our first guests arrived.

Shawn was the first to show, and we showed off the pond while we talked about gardening and a little bit of politics.

Matthew arrived a little later and it was time for another tour, this time taking the full circuit around to show off the bee garden and the future site of the community garden.

My son Frank arrived and we decided that was a good time to burn some things in effigy of sadness and celebration of 2020. A picture of our dog that we lost a few weeks ago, an "I voted" sticker, a BCF logo to celebrate a good season of harvest, and of course an N95 mask.

We continued to have an open conversation about politics...with healthy disagreements...without resorting to the hatefulness of similar conversations that occur online. I think part of it is that conversations are meant to be had face to face, where you can immediately see from someone's body language whether your point is being made or misconstrued, and part of it was because we agreed that political conversations should avoid conversations about actual politicians, but instead be about values, ideas, goals, philosophy.

Eventually we moved on to discussing musical theatre and pickup trucks. A few verses of songs from 1776 and Jesus Christ Superstar (two of my personal favorites) had been belted out by the time Chris and Cheryl arrived....which is always when a party can really start.

Beer, wine, good friends, good arguments, a little singing...all appropriately social-distanced but mask-free...and a roaring fire.

Definitely need to find time to repeat this event some time soon!

https://www.facebook.com/events/218074493077503/

  • Friday, November 27, 2020 at 1 PM – 5 PM
  • 606 N. Calumet Avenue, Valparaiso, IN 46383

What a wonderful awful year it's been - and as much as we've loved seeing you all during the gardening season, we can't wait for the holidays to start because that means once we get through them, this year is over.

So let's start the holiday season off right and send this year off in style with a bonfire at The Edge of Liberty.

Bring a chair and a drink and something small to burn in effigy to represent either something that happened this year worth celebrating or something you would rather forget.

item.title: Community Garden
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
While taking our daily walk around the property last week, I "convinced" my husband that a community garden in the middle of the turnaround hoop was the best use of the plot he's been amending with neighborhood leaf collection this fall. I put "convinced" in air quotes because he still has his doubts that it would be a successful endeavor, and is probably a little sad that it means 625 fewer delicata squash plants growing next season.

I wasn't sure it would be successful either, but with one post on Nextdoor.com, within two days I had nearly all of the 16 plots claimed.

I'm incredibly excited! While it's been great having amazing people come to our home garden every Saturday and enjoy our weekly harvests on our market day events during the summer, only a handful of people who come are also gardeners who can share the excitement of watching things grow. Even with those who are, I don't get to visit their work and share in their joy first-hand.

Next year is going to be amazing! I'm looking forward to making new friends who are just as dirty and sweaty as I am. I think even the winter will be fun as we communicate about what we're going to grow, making our growveg.com plan together, and purchasing and starting seeds.

Community Garden Rules and Responsibilities

  • There is no charge for your plot; Plots are 10x10
  • What you grow is yours to do with what you want as long as you tend it and clean it up at the end of the season; anything you leave behind will be disposed of properly.
  • No permanent structures or perennials as the plot will be amended and re-tilled each fall
  • All plot stewards should be available in late April to help set up intra-garden paths
  • We can help with seed-starting in our greenhouse if you provide materials
  • Garden is not fenced so try to avoid plants that attract wildlife; You can put up a temporary fence around your plot but you must take it down at the end of the season.
  • There is no electricity, running water, or bathroom facilities so plan your day accordingly
  • We will provide access to rainwater collection; bring your own watering cans
  • Please do not use chemicals. This is an organic farm.

item.title: Dreaming for the future
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
Unlike most people, we didn't have a plan for what we were going to do with our property when we purchased it. All we knew is that we didn't want it sold to someone who would replace all the goldenrod, sassafras, ramps, blackberries, sumac, black walnuts, garlic scapes, bee balm, and yellow rocket with asphalt. We didn't want to see the bible verse torn down and replaced with a clinic sign. We didn't want the children's graveyard from the 19th century desecrated by a parking lot.

For the last four years, it's been about uncovering what this land had to offer, guiding it into becoming something more, all while being good stewards of its natural bounty. Through my husband's incredibly hard work nearly every day of those four years, it's become a beautiful location to wander and wonder.

When I walk through it, I often dream of ways to share this place with others. When I first pull in, I imagine other cars in the small gravel parking lot he built to keep our own cars from sinking into the mud during the rainy season.

I can see people watching their children play in the beautiful lawn areas he keeps immaculate while enjoying a tail-gate picnic lunch under one of the mature pine trees he saved from overgrown vines and weeds.

I imagine people tending small garden plots we provided for them in the central turnaround hoop, growing things that they could never grow in their apartment container gardens in the now rich soil he's amended with leaves he mulched, bagged, and hauled in from a half dozen yards in the neighborhood for months.

I see people walking through the bee garden, teaching their children about nature and the interconnectedness of all life, while volunteers are tending the small plots of flowering perennials and annuals planted there to attract pollinators.

I see foragers wandering about collecting blackberries and scapes, watching bunnies run through the brambles to get away from dog-walkers, spotting deer tracks and bed-down locations on their hike.

I see friends and families and the entire community gathered around a bonfire, sharing drinks and laughs together and healing their souls from the damage of the online world.

I can visualize a small pavilion where local musicians can set up small concert events - local school orchestras and bands collecting donations for new instruments and uniforms - or an unplugged garage band selling their CDs.

I see a circle of canopies with local artists and crafters selling acrylic pours, handmade soaps, crocheted baby clothes, metal art, and woodwork next to tents where local organizations that promote education, conservation, and liberty teach others about their efforts and recruit volunteers.

I see the catch-basin finally filled with water so that we can truly call it a pond surrounded with beautiful wildflowers, lilies, and irises, with a small off-grid cabin near its northern shore. A family has rented it for the weekend. They can wake their children at sunrise to show them the deer that came for their morning drink then get them ready for a day of swimming and fishing and paddle-boating.

I picture a farmer's market stand near the road where people can come to buy locally grown organic food from our gardens and then stay a while to take a leisurely walk on a sunny Sunday afternoon.

I see all these things whenever I go to "the farm" and I am amazed by the work my husband has done to take us closer to the days when my dreams become reality.

item.title: July 2020 Update
item.dc:creator: admin
item.ns1:encoded:
Originally posted at https://www.batshitcrazyfarms.com/2020/07/07/the-edge-of-liberty-july-update/?source=2418

Been spending a lot of time up at The Edge of Liberty, our property on Calumet just north of 600. It’s rapidly becoming a beautiful space now that James got his dream tractor. We’re probably less than a month away from having a proper “parking lot” to welcome visitors.

We’ve learned a lot about gardening without water or electricity – and it’s incredible to me that the founding fathers of Indiana didn’t starve to death – at least the ones here in the Valparaiso moraine which is mostly clay and rock.

James has been filling up two 55 gallon barrels with the hose at home, hauling it up to the property with the ATV and trailer, and slowly and patiently watering with gravity pressure where the garden is low enough, and dipping watering cans where it’s not.

Some of our earliest planted rows had to be declared a complete failure, but luckily in the greenhouse we had extra bell peppers and a flat of “husk tomatoes” or ground cherries that came as a free gift with a seed order.

We moved out the one viable kohlrabi, and about eight kale plants that made it through this dry spell into the empty patches of the broccoli and brussel sprout row. Then we weeded and retrenched the two emptied row, filled them with compost from the Valparaiso compost site, and planted in 40 bell pepper and 20 ground cherry plants.

Today after work I hope to find what survived among the weeds in the cauliflower and cabbage row and fill in the remaining empty spaces in what we’ll call the “kale and friends” row, trench, compost, and plant in some excess leek starts and some beet seeds into that row in the same way.

Will need to wait for some rain before we can tackle the weeds that have taken over the hot pepper and potato rows since any attempt at pulling right now is leaving roots behind, and the soil is so hard it could break a hoe.  The other ten rows we were able to salvage with deep weeding, pruning, composting over the last week because the soil was still “almost” workable from the last rain.  

On the “parking lot” project, James and his tractor (or as I like to call it, his new girlfriend) moved a ton of soil into low patches in the hiking trails, pulled out trees and roots, tilled and flattened the space, and left a lovely 3 foot tall, five foot wide hill of compost and woodchips on the western edge. Together we planted out all of our remaining sweet potato plants (and are awaiting nine more babies from our prolific mama purple sweet potato to finish) and hope to see a lovely mound of gorgeous foliage there in about a month.  If we get any sweet potatoes, it will be a bonus – we just want the purple flowers. 

There’s a 15-20 foot wide space just west of that mound – left open as space for the free Norway spruce trees we got from an Arbor Day Foundation donation to grow into – that we’re going to seed in pumpkins – which should have just enough days to mature before Halloween.

Our modified Three Sisters garden isn’t going to be called a “failure” as much as it’s a learning experience and an opportunity to collect seeds from the corn, beans, and squash that were strong enough to thrive despite the weather and sub-standard soil.  We’re not babying the area with hand watering or weeding, so whatever makes it is going to be some genetically superior stuff worth propagating.

At the entrance, James has installed a wall of hibiscus trees repurposed from some weeding at my son’s house, re-homed volunteer sunflowers from the main garden, and cleaned up the hoop bed.  Wild garlic scapes are still trying to take over the area, but they do a nice job of keeping the bunnies at bay.

Bunnies are the enemy in the bee garden.  We finally got all the trapezoids and triangles dug out, composted, and planted, only to find that bunnies just love black eyed susan, asters, sunflowers, rhubarb, oxalis, ginger, peacock orchids, genovese basil (strangely, not the other three kinds of basil), columbine, and nasturtium.  We did find out that they do not like Irish spring soap – and 6 bars a month have been added to our Subscribe and Save list.  I may need to buy James a new food processor though.  Feels silly, but it has been effective to sprinkle soap shavings just outside the hosta border.  

The fishing line trick has definitely kept the deer out of the planted areas, but they seem to have taken over our future pond space.  I guess they just see it as a new meadow with tree coverage close by.  A momma robin has decided to take up residence in the lone pine tree in the bee garden and she gets quite mad if we choose to walk down the path near her tree.  The kill deer family moved out of the parking lot area last week once the babies were big enough to fly.

As for calling it a bee garden – it still hasn’t quite earned its name yet.  While the bees in our swarm trap do seem to like visiting the flowers that have started to bloom there, we haven’t had the right weather yet to plan their move-in date.  The hive stand is placed and leveled, enough hive equipment for three full sized hives are strapped down and waiting for final placement, and we’re just waiting for a night cool enough that they aren’t bearding outside the trap to move them to their new home.  We really do need to get this done by mid July so they have time to settle in and build up winter stores for sufficient heat mass.  Saving this particular colony is very important to us since they’re a swarm we caught late last summer, and they made it through the winter and spring in the trap – so these are some serious survivor stock.

Foraging opportunities abound on the property.  Last months ramps have been edged out by wild garlic scapes, sumac trees are setting flowers perfect for calming teas, and the blackberries are starting to fruit.  Please message us on Facebook if you’d like to forage, just to let us know you will be on the property, so that we don’t freak out if we see you there!

We hope The Edge of Liberty can become a space we can share with our friends and fans, for open air picnics and foraging and hiking.  Eventually some day we’d like to have a real farmer’s market or regularly scheduled art fair/acoustic music festival events there.  For now we’re just trying to get it to be a place we can bring prospective vendors to so they can see our vision and help us determine what other projects we need to do to make it a place they’d want to invest their time in.
